512453057e1c.headline: Nvidia soars 30% as Jensen Huang returns as CEO, dragging tech stocks along for the ride
body: Nvidia shares opened up 30% in New York on Monday after the chipmaker reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive with immediate effect, according to BBC News. The move added roughly $1 trillion to the company's market value.

The reversal is a whiplash one. Less than two weeks earlier, Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and Nvidia's shares had fallen significantly in the interim. The board voted unanimously to bring him back after what the company called a series of discussions and meetings with him.

The rally spread well beyond one company. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was up 6.5% in early trading. Microsoft and Amazon each gained nearly 4%, while Apple rose less than 2%. Other chipmakers did even better: Micron Technology jumped 19%, Intel climbed 14% and AMD gained nearly 7%. Much of the buying began in pre-market trading, before Huang's return was announced, following heavy tech losses on Friday.

Friday was ugly for Nvidia in particular. Its shares fell nearly 14% after Reuters reported, in a claim the BBC has not confirmed, that the US Securities and Exchange Commission was investigating the company's accounting practices. Monday's bounce comes on top of that cloud, not after it has cleared.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage XTB, called Huang the 'godfather' of AI with a 'talismanic influence over the sector'. She noted that although he holds no special voting shares, the directors evidently could not picture the company without him.
Nvidia sits at the center of the AI boom, since its chips are central to the industry. That is why one executive's job status can move not just one stock but a whole corner of the market.
512453057e1c.summary: Nvidia shares jumped 30% after the board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he resigned. The Nasdaq rose 6.5% in early trading as chip and tech stocks rallied.

0c1160d31848.headline: Moon Spuds Pass the Taste-Safety Test: Potatoes Grown in Fake Lunar Soil Are Safe to Eat
body: Potatoes grown in simulated moon soil are safe to eat, according to a new study from Oregon State University in the US, reported by Metro. The research, published in the journal npj Microgravity, suggests the humble spud could be a serious contender for future lunar menus.

The team, led by Professor Aymeric Goyer of the university's College of Agricultural Sciences and backed by Nasa funding, planted potatoes in lunar regolith simulants. Regolith is the loose rock and dust covering most of the moon's surface, and it contains very little organic matter. The researchers mixed in different levels of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich amendment made by using earthworms to break down organic material.

The amount mattered. Plants grown in simulants with 30% vermicompost matched the growth and development of those raised in Earth soil. Plants with no amendment were described as severely impaired, with stunting and underdeveloped roots, while those with 5% to 15% vermicompost recovered only partially.

Because moon dirt differs from place to place, the team tested five simulants representing both lunar mare and highland regions. They also grew potatoes in soil from Hermiston, Oregon, a region known for the highest potato yields in the world, as an Earth benchmark.

Safety was the other big question. Lunar regolith contains elevated levels of heavy metals, but the researchers believe organic matter helps by binding them, reducing damage to roots and growth. They found no statistically significant increase in glycoalkaloids, the natural potato toxins often linked to green discolouration under the skin.

The findings fit Nasa's Artemis goal of a sustained human presence on the moon, which would be far easier if food were produced there rather than shipped from Earth at great cost. The researchers say astronauts could carry a small amount of organic matter and then make more by converting food scraps and plant waste. Potatoes were chosen because they yield more calories per unit of land than many crops and are considered a practical staple for long missions.
0c1160d31848.summary: Oregon State University researchers found potatoes grown in simulated moon soil enriched with vermicompost matched Earth-grown plants and showed no significant rise in toxins, a step toward growing food for long lunar missions.
0c1160d31848.pixel_take: The Martian proved potatoes can survive on another world. Now science says the moon version won't poison you. Mash, boil, stick them in a lunar stew: the space race just got carb-loaded.
0c1160d31848.why_it_matters: Resupplying a lunar base from Earth is hugely expensive, so any way to grow food on site could cut mission costs. That matters for the commercial and government space sector, and for anyone watching the economics of long-term space exploration.
key_points: Potatoes in simulated lunar soil with 30% vermicompost grew as well as in Earth soil.
No statistically significant rise in glycoalkaloid toxins was found, despite heavy metals in regolith.
The work supports Nasa's Artemis aim of producing food on the moon instead of relying on resupply.

9329f8e154dd.headline: Big Bao Swallows Little Bao in a Cosmic Pac-Man Merger Near Andromeda
body: Astronomers have caught a giant star eating its smaller companion on the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, according to a new paper in the journal Nature. The merged star has been nicknamed Bao, and it may have been effectively rejuvenated by the meal.

The victim, dubbed Little Bao, had about 0.7 times the mass of the Sun. Its host, Big Bao, was a supergiant roughly seven times the Sun's mass, with a radius 350 times larger and a brightness about 18,000 times greater. Lead author Viraj Karambelkar's team says the pair had orbited each other for thousands of years before the collision.

What makes this special is the timing. Stellar mergers are hard to predict, so they are rarely seen live. The team flagged something odd in February 2023, using data from NASA's now-retired NEOWISE mission. Later telescopes tracked the star brightening and shedding dust, and the Zwicky Transient Facility recorded the eruption on 17 October 2025.

The James Webb Space Telescope then observed Bao on 24 December 2025, just 47 days after the eruption peaked. The researchers say that is the earliest follow-up of an event like this. Webb's mid-infrared data revealed the dust the larger star had released over hundreds of years.

The merger also moved fast. Once Little Bao touched the giant's surface, it took only seven orbits, about seven years, to finish the job. Other known mergers involving smaller stars have taken thousands of orbits. Co-author Kishalay De described it as almost like a bomb going off inside a living star.

The process is called common envelope evolution. Sometimes both stars survive and later become neutron stars, black holes, supernovae, gravitational-wave sources or millisecond pulsars. Here, simulations showed Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao's core. Scientists say more observations are needed to pin down Bao's final properties.
9329f8e154dd.summary: Astronomers watched a supergiant star swallow a smaller companion near Andromeda, with the James Webb Space Telescope capturing the aftermath just 47 days after the eruption peaked, according to a new Nature paper.
9329f8e154dd.pixel_take: Little Bao went from binary partner to main course in seven years. Somewhere, a very patient supergiant is still chewing, and astronomers are taking notes.
9329f8e154dd.why_it_matters: Rapid-response space observation is a growing field, and this event shows how coordinated telescope networks and fast data pipelines can catch fleeting events. Better models of stellar mergers also feed into understanding black holes and gravitational waves, which drive long-term science and tech investment.
key_points: A supergiant about 7 times the Sun's mass swallowed a 0.7-solar-mass companion near Andromeda.
Webb observed the merged star, Bao, just 47 days after the eruption peaked, the earliest such follow-up.
The merger took about seven years, far faster than other known mergers involving smaller stars.

The question still points to a real debate in personal finance. Some couples pool everything into joint accounts, others keep separate accounts, and many land on a hybrid, with a shared account for bills and individual accounts for personal spending. Each setup has its fans, and each can work when both partners are open about it.

Money is also one of the most common sources of tension in relationships, and secrecy tends to make it worse. Whether accounts are joint or separate, the habit that matters most is knowing where the household stands: what is owed, what is saved and what the plan is for retirement.

The letter also shows how much has changed in six decades. Arrangements where one spouse works outside the home and the other manages the household were common in 1970. Today, two-income households are far more common, and many partners arrive with their own savings, debts and financial habits, which makes separate accounts feel natural to some.

7959f46d944f.headline: Passenger sues driver over chicken-induced braking, loses and is ordered to pay costs
body: A woman in Singapore who sued her private-hire driver after he braked hard to avoid a car that had stopped for a chicken has lost her case. According to Metro, citing CNA, she was ordered to pay S$15,000 (about £8,700) in legal costs.

The incident happened on February 19, 2024, on Holland Road. Ms Yvonne Chen Qianyun was a passenger in a car driven by Mr Tan Teng Kiat. A chicken wandered in front of the vehicle ahead, which braked, and Mr Tan then braked too to avoid hitting it.

Ms Chen, whose injuries were not specified in the judgment, sued for negligence. She argued he had not left enough space and had stopped more forcefully than needed. Mr Tan said he was driving at around 50km/h, about 10 metres behind the other car, and had enough room and time to stop safely.

He also told the court that Ms Chen had first asked whether he had noted the number plate of the car in front, because she wanted to pursue that driver over her worsening back pain. He said she even asked him to be a witness, before later deciding to sue him instead.

Judge Ng noted that Ms Chen had at least two other cases pending in the district court, both over separate road accidents: one in September 2022 involving a private-hire car, and one in October 2024 involving her husband's car. She was a passenger in both.

The judge accepted she was an innocent passenger, but said the driver was not to blame. The law, the judge said, does not look for someone at fault for every loss, and some losses must lie where they fall. The chicken crossing was, in the judge's words, part of the 'vicissitudes of life'.
7959f46d944f.summary: A Singapore passenger who sued her private-hire driver for braking to avoid a chicken-related stop lost her case and must pay S$15,000 in costs. The judge called it part of life's vicissitudes.

39e3d33fb9cf.headline: Voyager 1 hits one light-day from Earth, the farthest any human-made object has ever strayed
body: NASA's Voyager 1 probe has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, according to UPI. That makes it the first human-made object in space to get that far from home.

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us, so a signal from Voyager 1 now needs a full day to cross the gap. Send it a message and you will wait roughly a day for it to arrive, then another day for the reply.

The milestone caps a decades-long journey. UPI reports that the probe has explored both the solar system and the interstellar medium beyond it, the thin space between stars that lies outside the Sun's immediate influence.

The material available for this story is brief, so details on the exact date of the crossing and the probe's current condition are not covered here. The headline fact is simple: nothing built by humans has ever been this far away.

For context, Voyager 1 is a veteran of an era when spacecraft were built to last on very modest computing power. It is a reminder that long-term engineering, patience and a good dose of luck can outlast several generations of gadgets, most of which struggle to survive a phone upgrade cycle.
39e3d33fb9cf.summary: NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth, a distance light needs 24 hours to cross, according to UPI.
39e3d33fb9cf.pixel_take: Voyager 1 is so far away that even its replies to 'u up?' arrive a day late. Still more reliable than most of our gadgets after two years.
39e3d33fb9cf.why_it_matters: Voyager 1 shows the payoff of long-horizon investment in space science and engineering durability. Data from interstellar space can't be gathered any other way, and it informs future deep-space mission design, a field with growing commercial and government interest.

Signals take about 24 hours to travel one way at that distance.
The probe has explored both the solar system and interstellar space, per UPI.

d5056aa77c07.headline: London's Newest Estate Agent Sells Gingerbread Homes, and the Only Mortgage Is Your Sweet Tooth
body: A gingerbread 'estate agent' has opened in Bloomsbury, central London, offering visitors a look at miniature edible houses. According to Metro, the pop-up, called Crumbs, Coffee & Co, opens on November 18 at 43 Store Street.

The tiny properties were made by baker Jenny Pasha, who spent 150 hours crafting houses that reflect popular architectural styles found across London. The star attraction is a model of the Shard, which on its own took 60 hours of baking and building.

The project is a promotional stunt from Nescafé. The brand says a survey found Brits name gingerbread as their favourite winter flavour, ahead of cinnamon, salted caramel, pumpkin spice and spiced apple.

The timing is deliberate: Nescafé is bringing back its Gingerbread Flavour Latte after a ten-year break, which it says followed fan petitions and social media requests. Visitors can collect a freshly brewed one for free, and entry to the pop-up costs nothing.

Ingrid Hayes, marketing director for Nescafé UK and Ireland, said research shows people want simple, affordable ways to bring joy to their winter routine. She said the pop-up gives fans an immersive way to celebrate the flavour while bringing café-style warmth into their own kitchens.
d5056aa77c07.summary: Nescafé has opened a free gingerbread 'estate agent' pop-up in Bloomsbury, London, showing handmade edible houses and a Shard model, to launch the return of its Gingerbread Flavour Latte after ten years.

d5056aa77c07.why_it_matters: Brands are leaning on immersive pop-ups and nostalgia to make seasonal products feel like events, often cheaper than traditional advertising and perfect for social sharing. 953bd48224b8.headline: Berlin brand's LA\VIK tabletop fireplace turns Norway's national rock into a blue-flashing flame show
body: Berlin design brand glør has built a tabletop fireplace called the LA\VIK around larvikite, a 295-million-year-old stone that is Norway's national rock, according to Yanko Design. The product recently took Top Design in the Home Product Design category at the 2026 European Product Design Award, run by the Farmani Group.

The trick is in the stone. Larvikite's feldspar crystals contain microscopic alternating layers that reflect light as a silvery blue sheen, an effect called labradorescence. Glør piles rough chunks over pale sand in a tall borosilicate glass cylinder, with a bioethanol flame rising from the middle. As the flame flickers, different crystals catch the light and flash blue, which is a notch more refined than the black lava rock many rivals use.

Practicalities are covered too. The fireplace needs no chimney or power cord, and glør describes the burn as smokeless. It comes in an 11-inch Studio size (about 17.6 pounds) and a 15-inch full size (about 31 pounds), with the weight deliberately low to keep it stable. A flame control dials the fire down and a lid snuffs it out. The brand lists up to two hours per fill for the Studio and three for the larger model.

On safety, glør says independent testing to EN 16647, the European standard for decorative alcohol-fueled fireplaces, covered stability, fuel containment and surface temperatures. It says the flame went out in under 10 seconds in testing and recommends a ventilated room of at least 130 square feet. Those are the brand's claims, so shoppers may want to read the fine print.

The Studio starts at €220, roughly $255, in colorways including Silver, Silver-Black, Black and Black-White. The name nods to Larvik, the Norwegian town that gave the stone its name, while glør itself comes from the Norwegian word for an ember.
953bd48224b8.summary: Berlin's glør won a 2026 European Product Design Award for the LA\VIK, a bioethanol tabletop fireplace using Norwegian larvikite, whose crystals flash blue in firelight. The Studio size starts at €220.
953bd48224b8.pixel_take: Finally, a rock with better lighting than most of us. Norway's national stone gets a side gig as a coffee-table disco, and unlike lava rock, it doesn't look like it survived a barbecue.
953bd48224b8.why_it_matters: Premium home decor is a growing niche where design awards and materials storytelling justify prices well above basic alternatives. It shows how small brands turn a single material into a product with a brand story. For buyers, the safety standard and fuel costs matter as much as the looks.
key_points: glør's LA\VIK fireplace won Top Design in Home Product Design at the 2026 European Product Design Award.
It uses larvikite stone, whose crystals flash blue, with a bioethanol flame in a borosilicate glass cylinder.
The Studio size starts at €220 (about $255); the brand cites EN 16647 testing.

5b5a2db04132.headline: Fed's Williams Hints Rate Hikes Are Coming, But Says Don't Expect a Sprint
body: New York Fed President John Williams said Monday that the central bank still has work to do on inflation, signaling that higher interest rates are likely "over time" rather than all at once, according to CNBC. He spoke at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York.

Williams, one of the most influential voices at the Fed, said he expects inflation to move closer to the 2% target in 2027 and to hit it the following year. He called getting back to that goal "100% essential" and said it must happen in a timely and sustained way.

He pointed to several sources of price pressure: the conflict in Iran, demand for goods tied to the AI build-out, and tariffs, whose effects he said have largely abated. He said there is "little evidence" that AI will become a source of more persistent inflation.

In his prepared remarks, Williams noted that monetary policy cannot move ships or reopen pipelines and refineries. It can, he said, keep those shocks from turning into broader or lasting inflation or from eroding inflation expectations.

He did not directly address the next Fed meeting on Dec. 8-9. CNBC reports that markets fully price in a quarter-point rate increase from the current 3.75%-4% target range. Williams said data since the October meeting show the economy remains strong and inflation continues to run too high.

Fed officials are reportedly split on pace, with some pushing for faster action and others, Williams among them, favoring a measured approach. His speech is expected to be the last major policy statement from a Fed official before the December decision.
5b5a2db04132.summary: New York Fed chief John Williams said more work is needed on inflation and that higher rates will come over time. Markets fully price in a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting, CNBC reports.
5b5a2db04132.why_it_matters: Higher rates make borrowing costlier for mortgages, car loans and credit cards, while potentially supporting savings yields. Williams' measured tone suggests the Fed prefers steady steps over shocks, which matters for stock and bond market expectations heading into December.
key_points: Williams says higher rates are likely "over time" to bring inflation back to 2%.
He expects inflation to near target in 2027 and hit it the following year.
Markets fully price a quarter-point hike from the 3.75%-4% range at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.

eca24540e663.headline: GTA VI hacker Arion Kurtaj gets seven years, then walks out on license
body: Arion Kurtaj, the hacker who broke into Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games, has been sentenced to seven years in prison but released on license, according to The Verge, citing the BBC. He pleaded guilty last week to hacking Rockstar and other companies, including Uber and Revolut.

In 2022, after breaching Rockstar, Kurtaj leaked 90 videos of the then-unreleased game. That was years before GTA VI reached the public, which happened last week, so the leaks spoiled a party that took a long time to be thrown.

The sentence comes with strings attached. Kurtaj is barred from using Telegram and Discord under a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order, the BBC says. He had already spent time in a hospital because of his autism, and in prison, before sentencing.
Sky News reported the judge's words: "You are obviously a very talented young man." The judge urged him not to waste those talents by spending the rest of his life in and out of prison.
Meanwhile, Rockstar's game has done just fine. GTA VI launched to positive reviews, and the studio said it made $3.79 billion on its first day of sales, according to the report.
eca24540e663.summary: Arion Kurtaj, who hacked Rockstar Games and leaked 90 GTA VI videos in 2022, got seven years but was released on license, with a five-year ban on Telegram and Discord.
eca24540e663.pixel_take: The leaks were supposed to spoil GTA VI. Rockstar still pulled in $3.79 billion on day one, so the spoilers had roughly the impact of a sneeze on a hurricane.
eca24540e663.why_it_matters: Breaches at big game studios and fintech or ride-hailing firms show how costly security failures can be, even when the business itself survives. Rockstar's record first-day sales show a leak rarely dents demand for a mega-franchise, but the legal and security bills still land on companies.

body: Jensen Huang is returning as chief executive of Nvidia, according to The New York Times, and the way it happened is raising eyebrows. The company's board had said he would not be back, but President Trump, who pushed for his reinstatement, effectively overrode that decision, governance experts told the paper.

The details are thin in the material available, so a few things remain unclear, including the circumstances behind Mr. Huang's departure and the mechanics of how his return was arranged. What the Times reports is the core tension: a board announced one outcome, and a political figure's pressure produced another.

That is the part governance specialists find notable. In the standard corporate playbook, a board's job is to hire, fire and oversee the chief executive on behalf of shareholders. A president lobbying for a particular executive to be reinstated sits well outside that script, and experts quoted by the Times read the result as the board being overridden.

For context, Nvidia is one of the most closely watched companies in technology, and its leadership is a big deal for investors who treat its fortunes as a barometer for the artificial intelligence boom. Questions about who actually holds the power to pick its chief executive are therefore not an academic matter.

What happens next is worth watching: how the board responds, whether shareholders ask for explanations, and whether this episode sets a precedent for political leaders weighing in on corporate leadership decisions.
929c81bf2aea.summary: Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang wouldn't return as CEO, but he is back after President Trump pushed for it, effectively overriding the board, governance experts told The New York Times.

7797d9dd4147.headline: Idaho Man Juggles His Way Through 19 Miles on In-Line Skates for World Record

Doing both at once, for a distance that rivals a long-distance run, is a very different sort of workout.

af980158c300.headline: Dorchester Honors Susie the Wandering Cat With a Bronze Statue Fit for a Local Celebrity
body: A town in England has done what many cat owners already believe is overdue: it has cast a feline in bronze. Locals in Dorchester gathered for the unveiling of a statue of Susie, a wandering cat described as one of the town's most beloved residents, according to UPI.

The material available gives few details beyond that. UPI's report says residents turned out for the ceremony, which suggests Susie's fan base is real, organized enough to show up, and presumably not easily distracted by a passing bird.

Statues of animals are a long-standing civic tradition, and a cat that roams across a town is a natural candidate. A wandering pet tends to become a shared neighbor, greeted and fed by people who may never meet its official owner. Bronze, unlike a cat, stays where it is put, which is likely a relief to everyone who has tried to find Susie.

There is a practical side to this, too. Quirky local landmarks like this often become small attractions, giving residents a point of pride and visitors a reason for a photo stop. Whether Susie becomes a tourist draw remains to be seen, since the report does not say so.

What is clear is that Dorchester has chosen to honor a cat rather than a general or a politician. In a news cycle heavy with grim headlines, that is a refreshingly low-stakes use of public affection and, one assumes, some serious metalwork.

af980158c300.pixel_take: Susie has finally achieved what every cat believes is her birthright: a permanent pedestal, and humans standing around admiring her. She will still ignore them.
af980158c300.why_it_matters: Small stories like this show how local identity and community spending can center on charming landmarks. Public art and quirky attractions can quietly support local pride and foot traffic for nearby businesses, though this report gives no figures.

The episode also shows how closely politics and the AI boom now intertwine. f1f7ae156bfa.headline: Trump Administration Blacklists Megaspeed, the Singapore Firm Tied to the Nvidia Scandal
body: The Trump administration has added Megaspeed, a Singaporean company at the center of a scandal involving Nvidia, to the entity list, a U.S. trade blacklist, according to The New York Times. The move came after weeks of sparring among top officials over whether to take the step.

The entity list is a Commerce Department tool that restricts which companies can receive certain American goods and technology. Being placed on it generally means U.S. suppliers need government licenses to ship to the named firm, which can choke off access to sensitive products.

The source material available to us is thin: the Times' teaser describes Megaspeed as being at the center of an Nvidia scandal, but it does not spell out the allegations, and we are not going to guess at them. What it does make clear is that the decision was not smooth, with senior officials disagreeing before the listing went ahead.

That internal friction is itself a signal. Export controls on advanced technology sit at the crossroads of national security, trade diplomacy and the commercial interests of American chipmakers, and those priorities do not always point in the same direction. A blacklisting that takes weeks of argument suggests the trade-offs were real.

For Nvidia, whose products are central to the global race in artificial intelligence, any enforcement action touching a foreign firm in its orbit is worth watching. More details on the reasoning and the scope of the restrictions should emerge as the full reporting and official notices circulate.
f1f7ae156bfa.summary: The Trump administration put Singapore-based Megaspeed, at the center of an Nvidia scandal, on the U.S. entity list after weeks of infighting among top officials, according to The New York Times.

86afad3ac324.headline: Russian drone strays into Polish airspace as Hungary's new PM plans a Ukraine trip
body: A Russian drone violated Polish airspace, just days after cruise missiles fell on the country, according to The Guardian's Europe live blog. Authorities are investigating what they described as "intentional activity", as tensions grow between Moscow and countries on Nato's eastern flank.

The material provided gives few further details on the incident, so key questions remain open, including where the drone entered and what it was doing. What is clear is that the episode follows the earlier missile incident, which makes the pattern harder to wave away as a one-off.

In a separate development reported in the same live coverage, Hungary's prime minister Péter Magyar announced a visit to Transcarpathia, the border region of Ukraine, for talks with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said on Facebook that he would travel with foreign minister Anita Orbán and visit several Hungarian institutions.

Magyar said it would be the first visit to Ukraine by a Hungarian prime minister since 2015. Transcarpathia is home to some 60,000 ethnic Hungarians and was one of the flashpoints in Hungarian-Ukrainian relations under the previous government of Viktor Orbán.

The trip follows Hungary dropping its opposition to opening the remaining "clusters" in Ukraine's EU accession talks, as reported by Euronews. Magyar appears to be seeking a more constructive relationship with Kyiv, a notable shift in tone from the previous government.
86afad3ac324.summary: A Russian drone violated Polish airspace days after cruise missiles fell on Poland, and authorities suspect intentional activity. Separately, Hungary's PM Péter Magyar plans a Ukraine visit.
86afad3ac324.why_it_matters: Security incidents on Nato's eastern flank raise risk premiums for regional markets, defense spending and energy. Hungary's softer stance on Ukraine's EU bid could speed enlargement, with long-term implications for European trade and funding.

2fd1319d90d1.headline: Pterodactyls over Mexico? Experts say the viral flying 'dinosaur' clips look more AI than Jurassic
body: Videos claiming to show pterodactyls flying over Ciudad Juárez, in Mexico's Chihuahua state, have gone viral in recent days, and experts consulted by Metro say the footage shows signs of AI generation rather than a prehistoric comeback.

The clips spread on X, Instagram, Facebook and Threads after Mexican journalist and UFOlogist Jaime Maussan shared them. Most show winged shapes soaring over Abraham González International Airport or perched on radio towers. One was said to come from a home security camera in Juárez Valley.

Maussan suggested the creatures might have slipped through 'interdimensional portals' in the Juárez Valley. His YouTube show Interestelar also aired a video said to be filmed by a boy on November 7 in the Felipe Ángeles neighbourhood, with a claim that the creature grabbed a dog and then dropped it. He added they were probably pteranodons, not pterodactyls.

Metro put the clips to two AI specialists. Nathan Marlor of Version 1 said the wings change shape from frame to frame, at times seeming to sprout a third wing, and that the wingbeats repeat identically, which real animals do not do. Snopes and local authorities have also noted that pterodactyls have been extinct for millions of years.

Detection software was less decisive. A VerifyLabs.AI report came back inconclusive, but co-founder Ruth Azar-Knupffer said that does not make the clips real. Grainy, compressed footage hides the telltale signs of synthetic media, and bad actors sometimes keep resolution low on purpose.

Azar-Knupffer warned that a few people believing a flying reptile story may seem quaint, but the broader problem is serious: as fake video improves, it erodes people's ability to tell real from fake, with consequences from personal relationships to elections.
2fd1319d90d1.summary: Viral videos of 'pterodactyls' over Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, show hallmarks of AI generation, experts told Metro. Detection tools were inconclusive, which experts say proves nothing about authenticity.
2fd1319d90d1.pixel_take: The only thing extinct here is the idea that seeing is believing. The wings changing shape mid-flap is a pretty good clue that this dinosaur was rendered, not hatched.
2fd1319d90d1.why_it_matters: Synthetic video is getting good enough to fool both people and detection software, which raises risks for fraud, market-moving hoaxes and elections. Low-quality, compressed clips are a classic way to dodge scrutiny, so skepticism about viral footage is now a basic financial and civic skill.
key_points: Viral clips claim to show pterodactyls over Ciudad Juárez, Mexico.
Expert Nathan Marlor points to wings that change shape and identical wingbeats as signs of AI.
A VerifyLabs.AI check was inconclusive, which does not prove the footage is real.

76dfc11a87d6.headline: ChatGPT's new GPT-6.2 Sol reads photos better and can offer to watch prices for you
body: OpenAI has rolled out a chat-tuned version of GPT-6.2 Sol to the Chat tab in ChatGPT, according to Digital Trends. The rollout began on November 23 and covers Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users. Free and Go users are not included yet.

The release comes less than a week after OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol in ChatGPT Work and Codex. OpenAI describes Sol as built for everyday work, while Astra is its frontier model for complex work. The models powering Work and Codex are not changing with this release.

OpenAI's release notes say the Chat version is better at following detailed instructions, reading details in photos and searching the web. It can help compare hotels by price and location, and pick up finer details in images, such as text or symbols. Ask whether something is on sale and it may offer to let you know when the price drops.

OpenAI shared test numbers for the Chat tab. Image understanding scored 71.7 percent, up from 47.4 percent for GPT-6. On especially challenging prompts, instruction following reached 78.1 percent, up from 62.5 percent. These are the company's own results, not independent benchmarks.

If your model picker shows GPT-6.2, the Latest option now uses it across all four thinking modes: Instant, Medium, High and Extra High. The Pro level still runs GPT-6 Pro, since there is no GPT-6.2 Pro yet. Enterprise access depends on workplace admin settings.
Anyone still on GPT-5.6 Sol can keep using it in Chat until OpenAI retires it on December 23. GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra also leave Work and Codex on that date.
76dfc11a87d6.summary: OpenAI is rolling out a chat-tuned GPT-6.2 Sol to ChatGPT's Chat tab for paid users. It follows instructions and reads photos better, and can offer to alert you when a price drops.
76dfc11a87d6.pixel_take: An AI that offers to watch a price for you is the first chatbot that might actually save you money instead of just talking you into the upgrade.
76dfc11a87d6.why_it_matters: Assistants that track prices and read photos move chatbots toward practical shopping help, which could change how people compare and buy. The paid-tier-first rollout and the December retirement of older models show how quickly AI subscriptions keep shifting under users' feet.
key_points: GPT-6.2 Sol is now in ChatGPT's Chat tab for Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users.

In plain terms, the guidance covers the cushion of assets a trading venue must hold to keep the lights on and absorb shocks. Until now, that cushion has typically been built from traditional holdings. Under the staff position as described by Cointelegraph, three crypto categories can now take a seat at the table: Bitcoin, Ether and payment stablecoins.

The source material is thin on details, so several things remain unclear from the headline and teaser alone: how the assets would be valued, whether any limits or haircuts apply, and which exchanges are in scope. Readers should watch for the full text of the guidance before drawing firm conclusions.

One general caveat is worth keeping in mind. Staff guidance from a regulator generally signals how the agency's staff view an issue, but it is not the same as a formal rule voted on by commissioners. It can still shape industry behavior, since firms often prefer to know where the regulator stands before changing their balance sheets.

Context matters here too. Bitcoin and Ether are known for price swings, while payment stablecoins aim to hold a steady value. Counting such different assets toward reserves raises the obvious question of how a regulator weighs stability against volatility. That is the kind of detail that separates a symbolic nod from a real shift in how exchanges are run.

e7a813ea5cf8.headline: Malaysia to send back over 6,500 Myanmar refugees days after ICJ genocide ruling
body: Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced to parliament on Tuesday that Malaysia will return more than 6,500 refugees to Myanmar in a new round of repatriations, according to Al Jazeera. The plan covers a large share of the Rohingya and other Myanmar nationals currently in the country.
The timing is striking. The announcement came five days after the International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled that Myanmar's security forces committed genocide against the Rohingya minority.

Anwar said 1,500 people will be returned on three navy vessels on December 6 and 7. A further 5,303 will be flown back during December, with the Myanmar government covering the cost, he told lawmakers.

Malaysia has long been a haven for people fleeing Myanmar, but it has grown frustrated, calling the hosting burden a financial and security risk. Anwar acknowledged that many asylum seekers were victims of atrocities by the Myanmar regime, but said Malaysia can no longer afford to host them and that hopes of resettlement in third countries had not worked out.

Rights groups are worried. In late September, around 1,500 migrants were sent back under an opaque scheme, and Malaysia later said it would seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of returnees were held in military detention. Anwar did not mention that request in his speech. Rights groups also criticised Malaysia for hosting Myanmar's former junta chief-turned-President Min Aung Hlaing last month, saying it risked legitimising his government.

Anwar framed his engagement with Myanmar's leadership as protecting Malaysia's interests and in line with the ICJ ruling, which said Myanmar must allow and facilitate safe, voluntary and dignified returns. As of August, UNHCR data showed 225,740 refugees and asylum seekers registered in Malaysia, about 90 percent from Myanmar.
e7a813ea5cf8.summary: Malaysia will repatriate over 6,500 Myanmar refugees in December, Anwar Ibrahim said, days after the ICJ found Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. Rights groups fear for returnees' safety.
e7a813ea5cf8.why_it_matters: Host countries are weighing the costs of long-term refugee support against humanitarian obligations, and Malaysia's move shows how fiscal pressure shapes migration policy. It also touches regional diplomacy and Malaysia's ties with Myanmar's government.
key_points: Over 6,500 Myanmar refugees to be returned, by navy ships on Dec 6-7 and by air in December
The plan follows an ICJ genocide ruling against Myanmar five days earlier

03553c710308.headline: Trump Puts Jensen Huang Back at Nvidia's Helm, Sidelining Security Warnings, NYT Says
body: President Trump has made what The New York Times calls an extraordinary intervention involving Nvidia, moving to put chief executive Jensen Huang back at the helm of the company. The Times describes the step as the latest sign of Trump's indifference to warnings from his own intelligence agencies.

The material available to us is limited to the Times' headline and teaser, so the specifics of what the move involved, how it unfolded and what the intelligence agencies actually warned about are not detailed here. According to the Times, the national security concerns were pushed aside rather than resolved.

The framing matters because Nvidia sits at the center of the global race over advanced computing. Its chips power much of today's artificial intelligence boom, which is why governments treat the company as both an economic crown jewel and a strategic asset.

In general terms, tension between security agencies and commercial priorities is not new. Intelligence and defense officials tend to favor caution about who controls critical technology, while business leaders and some political figures stress growth, competitiveness and market access. The Times' account suggests that in this case the second camp prevailed.

Readers should treat the story as an analysis of presidential decision-making as characterized by the Times, and watch for further reporting that fills in the details, including any response from the White House, Nvidia or the intelligence community.
03553c710308.summary: The New York Times reports that President Trump's move to put Jensen Huang back at Nvidia's helm caps a pattern of disregarding his own intelligence agencies' warnings. Details remain thin in the available material.
03553c710308.pixel_take: When the spy agencies wave a red flag and the president files it under 'decorative,' the chip business gets its captain back and the briefing binder gets a very nice coaster.
03553c710308.why_it_matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, so decisions about its leadership and security oversight can move markets and shape chip policy. If political priorities override intelligence warnings, investors and tech firms face greater uncertainty about how technology rules will be set.
key_points: The NYT says Trump moved to put Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia.
The Times frames it as part of Trump's indifference to his intelligence agencies' warnings.
Full details were not available, so key specifics remain unclear.

a81650fc7bbb.headline: Ex-OpenAI Employee Accused of Bugging Meetings Allegedly Had Saudi Government Ties, Prosecutors Say
body: Prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan, the former OpenAI employee charged with hiding a recording device at the company's headquarters, was allegedly in frequent contact with people affiliated with the Saudi government. The claim comes from a filing opposing his bail request, according to Engadget, which cited Bloomberg. A bail hearing in San Francisco was due to be held on the day of the report.

Prosecutors argue Alfozan could flee to his native Saudi Arabia because his ties to the United States are weak. They also say authorities found hundreds of audio files on his computer. Dozens were reportedly recordings of meetings and conversations at OpenAI during September 2026, and many involved what prosecutors called possible trade secrets.

The alleged paper trail is oddly tidy. Prosecutors say he uploaded some recordings to Dropbox, made AI-generated transcripts, sorted them by date and renamed files by content. Investigators also reportedly found phone photos of a document about a "strategic partnership" marked confidential.
The case began in October, when OpenAI staff found a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room. Alfozan was arrested and fired the same day, the report says.

Alfozan denies stealing trade secrets for Saudi Arabia and is asking the court to set a $1 million bond. According to Bloomberg, US District Judge Vince Chhabria has already questioned whether Alfozan should stay in custody without evidence supporting a more serious charge. The allegations about Saudi links remain just that: claims in a prosecution filing.
a81650fc7bbb.summary: Prosecutors say a former OpenAI employee charged over a hidden recording device was in frequent contact with Saudi government-linked people. He denies stealing trade secrets, and a judge has questioned keeping him in custody.
a81650fc7bbb.why_it_matters: AI labs hold some of the most valuable confidential information in tech, from partnership terms to strategy. Alleged insider leaks raise security and espionage concerns that can affect investor confidence and how companies guard sensitive work.
key_points: Prosecutors allege Abdulrahman Alfozan was in frequent contact with Saudi government-affiliated people and could flee the US.
Authorities reportedly found hundreds of audio files, including September 2026 OpenAI meeting recordings, plus photos of a confidential partnership document.
Alfozan denies stealing trade secrets and seeks a $1 million bond; the judge has doubted keeping him in custody.

37cae4b73bcd.headline: Corporate landlords rise as small ones sell up, and renters may get a pricier two-tier market
body: England's rental market is slowly changing hands. According to BBC News, large institutions are piling into build to rent (BTR), where developers construct blocks of flats or family homes and rent them out themselves. Savills expects 2026 to be another record year for such investment, while many small landlords say they are being squeezed out.

The scale of the shift is still modest. Savills research from 2024 put institutional ownership at around 40% of rental homes in the US and Germany, but only 3% in the UK. Government data shows 83% of English landlords own four properties or fewer, covering 51% of tenancies. Yet BTR homes tripled between 2019 and 2025, and Grainger chief executive Helen Gordon thinks the sector could reach at least 10% within a decade.

Policy has pushed in that direction. Savills' Lucian Cook points to a decade of tax changes for small landlords, including curbs on mortgage interest relief and higher stamp duty on extra homes, followed by the Renters' Rights Act and tougher energy efficiency rules. The last two Budgets also raised taxes on rental income from next year, a change that hits individuals but not companies paying corporation tax. Cook says small landlords have had more stick than BTR has had carrot.

Then there is the price tag. BBC News compares a furnished studio in Grainger's Cardiff building at £1,265 a month with a furnished one-bedroom flat with a garden about 15 minutes away at £800. The pricier option comes with a gym, cinema room, roof terrace, concierge and a better energy rating. Gordon argues scale lets big landlords fund helplines and systems that small ones cannot.

Renters are split. Lexi Levens, an NHS nurse who was served a no-reason eviction notice in 2021, welcomes more professional landlords with fewer personal preferences. Clint Stevenson, who pays £550 a month in Ramsgate, loves his personable landlady and found BTR flats expensive and impersonal. Small landlord Kevin Barber says big property firms hold too much sway with government.

Meanwhile the supply problem remains. The Joseph Rowntree Foundation found a net 2.74 million homes joined the English rental market between 2000 and 2016, but only about 200,000 in the decade since. Many experts agree that building more homes is the real fix, though whether that happens is still an open question.
37cae4b73bcd.summary: Big developers are building more homes to rent while small landlords face tougher rules and taxes. BBC News reports BTR is still 3% of UK rentals but could grow, raising questions about prices, service and choice.
37cae4b73bcd.pixel_take: Rent a flat with a cinema room and a concierge, or one with a landlady who lets you walk her dog. England's housing market is now a choice between amenities and affection.
37cae4b73bcd.why_it_matters: Who owns rental homes shapes what tenants pay, what they get and how easily they can complain. Tax changes that favour companies over individual landlords could reshape where institutional money flows. Without more homes being built, higher-end rentals may not ease the squeeze on ordinary budgets.
key_points: Build to rent is about 3% of UK rentals, tripled since 2019, and could hit 10% in a decade.
Tax and regulatory changes have hit small landlords harder than corporate ones.
A Cardiff BTR studio costs £1,265 against £800 for a nearby one-bed, with amenities as the trade-off.

530eaa08afbc.headline: Nvidia Reinstates Huang, Stock Jumps a Third, and The Guardian Wonders if Tech's Gilded Age Is Ending
body: Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and the market cheered, lifting the company's share price by about a third, according to a Guardian analysis by Eduardo Porter published on November 24, 2026.

Porter writes that Huang appears to have been forgiven after a call from someone in the White House, possibly Donald Trump himself. The reports concerned Huang's alleged relationship with a potential Chinese spy and with a company employee. Trump said the board wanted to know whether there was a national security problem, and that he told them there wasn't.

The Guardian columnist argues the episode shows how much power a few AI-era founders hold. He draws a line to Sam Altman, who was fired by OpenAI's board and reinstated within weeks after an investor revolt. He also notes that the president owns a non-trivial number of Nvidia shares.

Porter compares today's tech leaders to the Gilded Age barons of railways and steel. Back then, he writes, magnates bought political influence through lobbying, campaign money and bribes, and enjoyed generous government support. He likens the federal subsidies to Elon Musk's companies to the railroad land grants of that era.

The piece also points to inequality: in 1913 the richest 1% took almost 18% of national income and held nearly 40% of wealth, shares similar to today's, he says. The Progressive Era that followed brought a federal income tax, antitrust law and new regulations, and the top 1% share of wealth fell below a quarter by the late 1970s.

Porter sees hope in the Democrats' midterm sweep. He notes that Huang is already set to testify before Congress over the scandal, and suggests executives may face more accountability. This is an opinion-driven analysis, and the Guardian itself says it is hard to know what is true at this stage.
530eaa08afbc.summary: A Guardian analysis says Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang, after a reported White House call, shows tech oligarchs' power. It asks whether Democratic midterm gains could end a modern Gilded Age.
530eaa08afbc.pixel_take: Nvidia's stock rose by a third after the CEO's comeback. Nothing says strong corporate governance like a market standing ovation and a phone call from the White House.
530eaa08afbc.why_it_matters: Nvidia sits at the center of the AI boom, so questions about its governance and political ties matter for investors and for chip policy toward China. A shift in Congress could bring more scrutiny, and possibly regulation, of the biggest tech firms.
key_points: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang and the share price rose by about a third, per The Guardian.
Trump said he told the board there was no national security problem; Huang is set to testify before Congress.
The analysis compares today's tech titans to Gilded Age barons and hopes for a Progressive-style correction.

99b6b00d1e57.headline: Ted Lasso Gets Season 5, Proving 'The End' Is Merely a Suggestion
body: Apple has renewed Ted Lasso for a fifth season, according to Engadget, which reported the news on November 24, 2026. The company announced the move in a press release, calling the show a global phenomenon returning to the pitch.

The announcement is a bit of a plot twist. Many viewers assumed the series was done after season three, and co-creator and star Jason Sudeikis said after that finale that it was the end of the story the team wanted to tell.

Then came season four, which swapped the men's AFC Richmond squad, the Greyhounds, for the Division 2 Lady Greyhounds. Engadget notes it didn't quite match the critical heights of the first two seasons, but it beat season three with a 90 percent Rotten Tomatoes critical rating.

Season four closed with the Lady Greyhounds promoted to the women's Super League, the team's ownership settled, and tidy send-offs for characters including Roy Kent, Keely, Coaches Lasso and Beard, Rebecca, and Alice Chilton. Apple has not said whether season five will follow the Lady Greyhounds or head somewhere else, and it offered no other details.

For Apple TV, the stakes go beyond one mustache. Engadget points out that Ted Lasso was the platform's first bonafide hit, setting a marker for later popular series such as Severance, Silo, The Studio, Pluribus and Widow's Bay.
99b6b00d1e57.summary: Apple has renewed Ted Lasso for a fifth season, per Engadget, despite earlier signs the show had ended. No plot details were given, including whether the Lady Greyhounds remain the focus.
99b6b00d1e57.pixel_take: Ted Lasso said the story was over, then came back twice. Believe in renewals, folks: the only thing stickier than a hit show is a streaming budget.
99b6b00d1e57.why_it_matters: Streaming services lean hard on proven hits because subscribers stick around for familiar favorites. Renewing a show that was supposedly finished shows how valuable a recognizable brand is to Apple TV's catalog. It also hints at how platforms weigh nostalgia against new, riskier shows.
key_points: Apple confirmed Ted Lasso season five in a press release.
Season four, centered on the Lady Greyhounds, earned a 90 percent Rotten Tomatoes critic rating.
No plot or cast details have been revealed yet.

a14278058cc9.headline: AI Picks AI Stocks: Investing.com Says Five Tech Names Still Have Up to 52% Upside
body: Investing.com published a markets piece on November 24, 2026, saying five tech stocks chosen by an AI-driven screen still carry as much as 52% upside as the artificial intelligence rally continues.

The headline describes the rally as having "erupted" and calls the five names "AI-picked tech winners." The full text of the article was not available to us, so we cannot say which companies made the list, how the upside figure was calculated, or over what period.

What we can say is the shape of the claim: the up-to-52% figure is the best case among the five, not an average, and it is a projection rather than a result. Upside estimates of this kind usually compare a current share price with a target price, and targets can change quickly when sentiment or earnings shift.

There is also some irony in the setup. Software is being used to pick the stocks of companies that build software, so the AI hype cycle is now feeding on itself. That does not make the picks wrong, but it is worth remembering that a model is only as good as the data and assumptions behind it.

For readers, the practical takeaway is to treat lists like this as a starting point for research. Check who is behind the numbers, how concentrated your portfolio already is in tech, and whether a rally this strong has already priced in much of the good news.
a14278058cc9.summary: Investing.com says five tech stocks picked by an AI-based screen still have as much as 52% upside amid the AI rally. The article's details were not available, so the names and method remain unknown.
a14278058cc9.pixel_take: An AI picking AI stocks is like a baker rating bakeries: possibly insightful, definitely not neutral. Maybe ask the robot for its error bars too.
a14278058cc9.why_it_matters: AI-themed stocks have been a major driver of tech market gains, so forecasts of big upside draw investor money quickly. But upside targets are estimates, not guarantees, and heavy exposure to one theme can magnify losses if sentiment turns.

The 52% figure is a maximum, not an average, and is a projection.

1125e0936921.headline: Google Lets AI Mode Peek Into Your Wallet, Read-Only, With Drive and Gemini Next
body: Google is connecting Google Wallet to the Personal Intelligence feature in AI Mode in Search, according to Digital Trends, which cited a new Google blog post. The Wallet link is rolling out now, and Google plans to add Drive and the Gemini app in the coming weeks.

The idea mirrors a feature Google brought to the Gemini app earlier this month, which breaks down expenses, spending categories and cash flow, and flags forgotten subscriptions. With Wallet connected to Search, users can map out financial milestones, look for ways to trim everyday spending, and squeeze more out of credit card perks such as rewards plans, travel benefits and cash-back categories, based on the cards linked in Wallet.

Google stresses the guardrails. Connecting apps is opt-in, and users can switch them on or off anytime in Search settings. Wallet access is read-only, so AI Mode can't move, manage or invest your money. In other words, it can judge your coffee habit but not touch the balance.

Drive and Gemini add different skills. With Drive connected, AI Mode can pull scattered details from PDFs, docs and sheets to help kick off projects, such as a personalized prep plan for tax season. The Gemini connection lets AI Mode build on ideas from earlier Gemini conversations, and vice versa.

To connect an app, users go to Google Search Settings and choose Search Personalization, or open the Connected Apps settings directly. Gmail, Calendar, Photos and Wallet are among the options. Google also plans to show a Personalization icon under personalized answers, revealing which app and data shaped the reply.

Eligibility has limits. Google's help pages say users must be 18 or older, have a personal Google Account, and have Search history and Personal Recommendations turned on. Availability varies by country and language. AI Overviews and AI Mode will also begin using recent search context in new threads, which can be turned off in Search Settings.
1125e0936921.summary: Google is rolling out an opt-in, read-only Wallet connection for Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, with Drive and the Gemini app to follow in the coming weeks, according to Digital Trends.
1125e0936921.pixel_take: Google's AI can now see your spending but not touch your money. Like a financial advisor stuck behind glass, tapping on it to point out the subscriptions you forgot.
1125e0936921.why_it_matters: Search is becoming a personal finance assistant, which could change how people track spending and use card rewards. It also raises the stakes on privacy settings, since more personal data sits one toggle away from an AI.
key_points: Wallet connects to AI Mode's Personal Intelligence now; Drive and the Gemini app follow in the coming weeks.
Access is opt-in and read-only, and AI Mode can't move, manage or invest money.
Users must be 18+ with certain settings on, and availability varies by country and language.

221782537b93.headline: Maryland Woman Hits Scratch-Off Jackpot Twice, Because Lightning Apparently Likes Her Address
body: A Maryland woman has won a $30,000 top prize from a scratch-off lottery ticket, according to UPI. It is not her first brush with scratch-off luck: less than a decade ago, she won $50,000 from another game.

That adds up to $80,000 in two wins, based on the figures in the report. The material provided does not say which game she played, where she bought the ticket, or what she plans to do with the money, so we will not guess.

Winning twice sounds like cosmic favoritism, but the math is more modest than it feels. Each ticket is an independent draw, so earlier wins do not make later ones more or less likely. With millions of players buying tickets, someone is bound to land a repeat prize eventually, and those stories make headlines precisely because they are rare to any one person.

For the rest of us, the lesson is the usual one. Lottery games are designed so that the house, in this case state lottery proceeds, comes out ahead over time. Scratch-offs are fun, but a financial plan built on them is more of a hobby than a strategy.
221782537b93.summary: A Maryland woman won a $30,000 top prize on a scratch-off ticket, less than a decade after winning $50,000 from another game, UPI reports.
221782537b93.pixel_take: Two big scratch-off wins in under a decade. Most of us can't even win the argument over which pen to use for scratching.
221782537b93.why_it_matters: Repeat winners make lottery odds feel friendlier than they are. Each ticket is an independent bet that, on average, costs players more than it pays. Treat scratch-offs as entertainment spending, not income.
key_points: A Maryland woman won a $30,000 top prize on a scratch-off ticket.
She won $50,000 from another game less than a decade ago.
Each ticket is an independent draw, so past wins do not improve future odds.

63c39b84f6e4.headline: Five-Star Claims, One-Star Reality: BBC Finds Dog Breeder Selling Sick Puppies at £2,000 a Pop
body: A BBC investigation has found that a Whitby, North Yorkshire breeder, Michael Estill of Mikjulora Dobermanns, kept advertising a five-star licence rating after his council downgraded him to one star, while selling puppies that later fell ill, according to the BBC. The downgrade came with his January licence renewal, roughly two months before the sales examined.

Katie Thornton of Harrogate paid £2,000 for a nine-week-old Dobermann called Ozzy. He coughed on the way home and was in a veterinary hospital with pneumonia within 48 hours. She says her vet bills now top £5,000. Other buyers described puppies with pneumonia, eye ulcers and heart problems, and one owner said her dog Bentley died aged three of a heart condition.

Vet reports for North Yorkshire Council from August and December 2025, seen by the BBC, listed dozens of concerns, including cramped cages and puppies that did not match their descriptions. The reports concluded the business was functioning outside the law. Even so, the council renewed the licence. It said the threshold for revoking it was not met on the available evidence, and that it was satisfied standards had significantly improved.

BBC reporters also filmed undercover at Estill's home. He declined to show where the puppies and their mother slept, which a former RSPCA chief vet, Dr Caroline Allen, called the most serious concern and a breach of regulations. She said two puppies had abnormal eyes. His licence and rating were not displayed either, despite government rules.

The problem looks wider. The BBC checked 806 English breeders rated one to four stars and found at least 15 advertising a higher rating than they actually hold. Among 573 breeders rated three stars or below, 541 showed no rating online at all. There is no official national list of licensed breeders and ratings, and not every council publishes them, so buyers often have only the seller's word. Allen described a nationwide wild west that makes it easy for consumers to be scammed.
63c39b84f6e4.summary: A BBC probe found a North Yorkshire breeder kept advertising five stars after a downgrade to one while selling sick puppies. It also found at least 15 other English breeders overstating ratings.
63c39b84f6e4.why_it_matters: A £2,000 puppy can turn into a five-figure vet bill when a seller's rating cannot be verified, and there is no central register to check. The case shows how weak oversight leaves buyers carrying the financial and emotional risk.
key_points: Breeder kept advertising five stars after a council downgrade to one star, the BBC found.
Buyers report sick puppies, with one owner's vet bills above £5,000.
At least 15 other English breeders advertised inflated ratings, and no official national list exists.

e45b9d3201a5.headline: Pennsylvania Measles Deaths Climb to Nine, Investing.com Reports
body: Measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania have risen to nine, according to a headline from Investing.com published on November 24, 2026.

The material available to us consists only of that headline. It does not say when the deaths occurred, where in the state they happened, who the victims were, or how many cases are linked to the outbreak, so we are not going to guess at those details.

What the headline does establish is the toll: nine deaths tied to measles in a single U.S. state. Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, and public health authorities have long noted that it spreads easily in communities where vaccination coverage is low.

Health outbreaks rarely stay a purely medical story. Large outbreaks can strain hospitals and local health departments, prompt school and workplace disruptions, and draw political attention to vaccination policy and public health funding. Investors tend to watch such developments for their effects on healthcare costs and on sectors such as healthcare services and vaccine makers.

Outbreaks can affect healthcare systems, public budgets and policy debates.

24384649709a.headline: Meta sends its Muse AI agent to the UK to brave the Christmas shopping crowds for you
body: Meta is launching its Muse AI assistant in the UK, pitching it as a way to hand off chores such as Christmas shopping, booking travel and sending emails, according to The Guardian. Muse works as a standalone app or inside WhatsApp.

The company says Muse has been a hit in the US, where it ranks first on Google's free app store and second on Apple's, with millions of downloads. British users can give their assistant a name, a look and a personality, then connect it to email, calendars and retailer apps. Meta's own examples include finding a cheaper energy deal, chasing a refund, renewing car insurance and sorting the school calendar.

Meta calls handing over your digital life to an agent "an act of trust" and says it has built in guardrails. Muse needs your approval before buying something or sending an email, only joins apps you permit, and cannot see your passwords or payment methods. A separate security agent checks its actions against the permissions you granted. Meta also says it does not share conversations with advertisers.
The company has signed deals with British businesses including Marks & Spencer, Currys, Sainsbury's and easyJet so Muse can navigate their sites more easily.

Not everything has gone smoothly. Reuters reported last week that Meta employees raised concerns about performance, including a reminder to reply to a message on Signal and a message containing random bank account balances. Meta says internal testing exists to catch such problems before public release, and it is understood most of the issues came from a bug that has been fixed.

UK regulators, including the Competition and Markets Authority and the Information Commissioner's Office, said last month that AI agents could unlock innovation but also amplify risks such as fraud, scams and misuse of personal data. Meanwhile Meta's chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, wrote on Sunday that keeping human control over far smarter AI is hard to imagine, and called safety and alignment work extremely urgent.
24384649709a.summary: Meta is launching its Muse AI agent in the UK, offering to shop, book travel and send emails with user approval. Reported glitches and regulator warnings about fraud and data risks tag along.
24384649709a.pixel_take: Meta's agent will brave the shops so you don't have to, though it may also remind you to answer your sister on an app you forgot you had.
24384649709a.why_it_matters: AI agents that can spend your money move chatbots from advice to action, which could reshape how retailers and travel firms win customers. They also raise real questions about fraud, privacy and who is liable when an agent gets it wrong.
key_points: Muse launches in the UK via app and WhatsApp, with retail and travel partners including M&S, Currys, Sainsbury's and easyJet.
Meta says purchases and emails need user approval, and Muse cannot see passwords or payment methods.
Reuters reported glitches, which Meta largely attributes to a fixed bug, while UK regulators flag fraud and data risks.

0d678abc5bd3.headline: Australia Moves to Hit Big Tech With Fines Up to 5% of Global Revenue Over Online Harm
body: Australia's government on Tuesday detailed a proposed digital duty of care law that could fine tech companies, including Google and Meta, up to 5 percent of their worldwide revenue if they fail to remove harmful content, according to Al Jazeera. The bill is expected to pass Parliament this week.

The jump is steep. The previously proposed penalty was 109 million Australian dollars ($72.2m), a sum that is small change for platforms earning hundreds of billions of dollars a year. Tying the fine to global revenue turns a rounding error into a line item that shareholders might actually notice.

The bill was agreed between the centre-left Labor government and the left-leaning Greens in the Senate. It would also let individuals sue platforms for enabling wrongdoing. Communications Minister Anika Wells called it "seismic reform" and said it would be delivered this week.

The law would replace a patchwork of enforceable codes drawn up by various industries, from messaging apps to search engines to AI chatbots, with one underlying rule requiring companies to proactively check for and stop harmful experiences. Targeted harms include child sexual abuse material, nonconsensual fake nude material, gender-based violence, self-harm promotion and terrorism. Australians aged 16 or older would also get the option to switch off algorithm-driven feeds.

Tech firms broadly share the goal of protecting children, but most oppose the bill because it gives some discretion to government officials over what counts as harmful content. Industry groups had already warned that the law might push platforms to over-remove content to avoid punishment, a concern that a bigger fine is unlikely to soothe.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese framed it as the next step after the under-16s social media ban, saying Australia was acting on the side of parents and children rather than foreign-owned tech companies. Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young said big tech had for too long filled feeds with addictive, harmful content.
0d678abc5bd3.summary: Australia is set to pass a law letting regulators fine tech firms up to 5% of global revenue for failing to remove harmful content, and letting people sue platforms. Industry objects to officials' discretion.
0d678abc5bd3.pixel_take: A fine based on global revenue is the rare penalty a trillion-dollar company can't expense as 'a cost of doing business' without someone in finance wincing.
0d678abc5bd3.why_it_matters: Fines pegged to global revenue could cost the largest platforms real money, and Australia often serves as a testing ground other governments watch. Investors and tech companies may face higher compliance costs and legal risk, plus pressure to rethink content moderation and feed design.
key_points: Fines could reach 5% of global revenue, up from a proposed A$109 million.
Individuals would gain the right to sue platforms for enabling wrongdoing.
Tech firms object to officials' discretion over what counts as harmful and fear over-removal.

That makes the reaction as much about positioning as about one chip executive. Corruption messaging is a familiar tool for a party out of power: it is easy to explain, hard to argue with in the abstract, and can attach to almost any story where business and government intersect.

Nvidia sits at an especially sensitive spot in that intersection. Its chips are central to the artificial intelligence boom, which means decisions touching the company draw attention from investors, regulators and politicians alike. d95aac037f5c.headline: Bitcoin ETFs Keep Bleeding Cash, Yet BlackRock's IBIT Shares Still Jump Nearly 5%
body: BlackRock's IBIT shares rose 4.85% on Monday, even as spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds kept losing money, according to Cointelegraph. Withdrawals from the funds have pushed net outflows for November to $4.71 billion.

The split is a good reminder that a fund's share price and its flows are two different things. Share price tracks the value of the underlying asset, so a gain in IBIT stock on a single day points to a stronger market for Bitcoin itself. Flows, by contrast, measure whether investors are putting money into the funds or pulling it out. On Monday, the two pointed in opposite directions.

The material provided doesn't break down which funds saw the biggest redemptions or what drove the day's price move, so the reasons behind the mismatch remain unclear. What it does show is that November has been a month of net selling by ETF holders, with $4.71 billion heading for the exits.

For context, spot Bitcoin ETFs have become one of the main channels through which traditional investors get exposure to the asset without holding it directly. That makes their flow figures a widely watched gauge of institutional appetite. Sustained outflows are often read as a sign of cooling demand or of investors reducing risk, though a single month does not settle the long-term picture.

For everyday investors, the takeaway is to avoid reading too much into one day's price pop. A rally can happen while big money is still heading out the door, and the two signals can take time to line up.
d95aac037f5c.summary: BlackRock's IBIT gained 4.85% on Monday even as Bitcoin ETF withdrawals pushed November's net outflows to $4.71 billion, according to Cointelegraph.

6a00ed68e54f.headline: Putin Vows 'Inevitable' Retaliation as Ukrainian Drones Keep Hammering Russian Refineries
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that retaliation is "inevitable" after Ukraine kept striking Russian oil refineries, according to Al Jazeera. He spoke at a Kremlin meeting with government officials and senior oil executives.

Putin said Kyiv was ignoring a direct request from US President Donald Trump to refrain from such attacks. Ukrainian strikes eased after Trump's mid-October declaration of an energy ceasefire, but picked up again in late October. Kyiv has said it will stop hitting Russian energy targets only when Moscow does the same. Putin also called for extra security measures at energy facilities.

The damage appears significant. Two industry sources cited by Reuters estimated that Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian refineries' combined crude processing by 45 percent since late October. Several Russian regions have introduced limits on retail sales of petrol and diesel, according to local media and authorities. Putin conceded the domestic fuel market remains difficult, but said petrol prices have stabilised after peaking in October.

The war is also spilling across other fronts. Poland accused Moscow of deliberately violating its airspace with a surveillance drone and said three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed on its territory on Friday. Moscow accused NATO member Estonia of hostile actions "on the verge of triggering open war" after Estonia closed their land border. A Russian cargo ship with military links caught fire in the Baltic after a Ukrainian-claimed drone attack, and Ukraine said it sank a Russian corvette in a Libyan port.

British security officials warned UK companies giving material support to Ukraine's armed forces to prepare for Russian sabotage attempts. Meanwhile, a Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia killed two people and wounded 40, including four children, Governor Mykhailo Semikin said. Russia's Defence Ministry, cited by Interfax, said it hit drone control sites and Starlink terminals in Sumy region.
6a00ed68e54f.summary: Putin threatened inevitable retaliation after Ukraine kept striking Russian refineries despite Trump's energy ceasefire appeal. Reuters-cited sources say refinery processing has fallen 45 percent, and regional fuel limits have appeared.
6a00ed68e54f.why_it_matters: Refinery outages squeeze Russian fuel supply and can ripple into energy markets and prices. An escalating tit-for-tat over energy infrastructure raises risks for fuel costs and for the wider regional security picture.
key_points: Putin says retaliation is 'inevitable' over continued Ukrainian refinery strikes.
Reuters-cited sources estimate a 45 percent drop in Russian refinery processing since late October.
Several Russian regions have limited retail petrol and diesel sales.

4059bf6cbecc.headline: White House asks Congress for $2B Artemis boost, giving NASA a bigger rocket budget and a very short runway
body: The White House on Monday night sent Congress a list of requested budget exceptions, known as funding anomalies, and among the largest non-defense items is $2 billion for NASA's Artemis moon program, according to Ars Technica. The money is meant to support a "higher rate of operations."

Technically, the request would lift Artemis's annualized funding rate to $9.8 billion, up from roughly $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026, a boost of about 25 percent. It would not hand NASA an extra $2 billion in one lump sum immediately. The list is dominated by defense items, including the Golden Dome missile defense program.

The backdrop is a budget standoff. Fiscal year 2027 began October 1, and the government has been running on a continuing resolution that expires December 11. Ars Technica reports that another stopgap looks the most likely outcome, pushing a real budget deal into the new year. The anomalies list tells Congress what the administration wants included in that stopgap, which the president would need to sign.

The request looks like a win for NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who arrived 11 months ago, after the fiscal 2027 budget request was already drafted. This is his first chance to shape budget priorities with the administration. The document says the added topline is needed without jeopardizing other priorities in the National Space Policy, which suggests the money is not meant to come out of areas like science.

The White House says the funds would go to supply chain acceleration through in-house manufacturing and modernization in areas such as suits, thrusters, SLS-related hardware, habitats and astronaut safety systems. It warns that without the money, activities would be delayed. The wording is broad, which gives Isaacman flexibility to attack the worst bottlenecks.

The challenge ahead is finishing the lunar landers being built by SpaceX and Blue Origin, a key untested piece of the mission. NASA is also helping Axiom Space with a lunar suit and supporting smaller companies building hardware for its Moon Base initiative, all of which face supply chain trouble. Ars Technica notes China's lunar ambitions are just as expansive, and it may land astronauts before NASA does.
4059bf6cbecc.summary: The White House asked Congress for $2 billion more for NASA's Artemis program in a stopgap budget, lifting its annual rate to $9.8 billion, to speed supply chains and in-house manufacturing, according to Ars Technica.
4059bf6cbecc.pixel_take: Nothing says space race like a budget fight over a stopgap bill. Rockets may be hard, but getting Congress to agree by December 11 might be the real heavy lift.
4059bf6cbecc.why_it_matters: Artemis spending flows to major aerospace contractors and a growing commercial space sector, so funding shifts can move business for suppliers and partners. The request also shows how the budget standoff, and likely another stopgap, shapes what government programs can actually spend. Competition with China adds geopolitical pressure to the dollars.
key_points: The White House wants Artemis's annualized funding rate raised about 25 percent, from roughly $7.8 billion to $9.8 billion.
The money would target supply chain acceleration and in-house manufacturing for suits, thrusters, SLS hardware, habitats and safety systems.
The current continuing resolution expires December 11, and another stopgap looks likely.
